meta.title: Bengali B2 Upper Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1,500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Bengali → English (see the Bengali, recall the meaning) and English → Bengali (see an English meaning, recall the Bengali). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1,500 words for an upper-intermediate learner, aligned to B2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main ideas of complex text on both concrete and abstract topics, including technical discussions in their field of specialisation' — a learner here is able to interact with a degree of fluency and spontaneity that makes regular interaction with native speakers quite possible without strain for either party, and to produce clear, detailed text on a wide range of subjects and explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for learners of Bengali, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 253 of the 1,500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — business and the economy, politics, the law and society, science and technology, language and the arts, the mind and character, the words of argument and evaluation, the land and the environment, health and the body, more precise description, how and when things happen, and verbs of action — and the other 1247 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Bengali, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. The deck teaches the standard colloquial language (cholito bhasha) shared by West Bengal and Bangladesh; where an everyday word differs between the two — জল and পানি for water, নমস্কার and সালাম for a greeting — both are taught. Every headword is printed in the Bengali script with a romanisation beneath it, Wiktionary's own (ô for the open o of the inherent vowel, ō where the o-sign is written, a dot under the retroflex letters, ẏ and ẇ for the glides: kôra, bhalō), so the deck can be studied before the script is fluent; the Bengali Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the script itself. Bengali has no grammatical gender. The 1079 nouns show their definite form ('the …', with -টা), their plural and their genitive ('of …'); the 47 verbs show their present, their past and their 'having done' form, where the stem's vowel changes and the irregular verbs show, and behind the All forms fold every tense by person, at the three levels of address — তুই intimate, তুমি familiar, আপনি polite. Real example sentences come with 174 of the 1,500 words, three apiece for 38 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, forms and romanisation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
